meta.title: Imbalance, cash-out and settlement
meta.subtitle: What happens to the difference between what a supplier contracted for and what its customers actually used.
meta.one_line: Every half-hour, each supplier's contracted volume is compared with what its customers actually consumed. The difference is cashed out at a single imbalance price, and the comparison is re-run for more than a year afterwards as real meter data replaces estimates.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. Everything on this page is a published feature of the GB energy market, readable by anyone — so it is readable by the simulated company too, the same way a real supplier reads the codes. Nothing here is an internal of the simulation.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: A supplier is settled on the difference between contract and consumption in every half-hour, at a price it does not choose and cannot see in advance — and because the consumption side arrives late and improves for over a year, a supplier's own accounts for a past period are an estimate that keeps being corrected.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
This is the part of the industry that most surprises people who assume a supplier knows what it sold.

On the day, nobody knows. Domestic meters are not all read half-hourly, and even smart data does not all arrive promptly. So settlement starts with **estimates** — profiles that say what a typical customer of a given class would have used in each half-hour, scaled to their annual consumption.

Real readings then arrive over months. Settlement is re-run, several times, each run using better data than the last. A supplier's volume for a half-hour last February is a number that moves.

Meanwhile the difference between contracted and consumed is charged at the **imbalance price** — which is set by what it cost the system operator to fix the system's own shortfall, not by anything the supplier did. In a tight half-hour that price can be extraordinary. A supplier that was short in exactly those half-hours pays it.

The result is that a supplier's cost of serving a customer is genuinely not knowable on the day it serves them, and any figure it publishes early carries a clock.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
**Single price cash-out.** GB settles imbalance at one price per half-hour for everyone — you do not get a better price for being long in the helpful direction. The price is derived from the actions the system operator actually took to balance, so it reflects real scarcity.

**Profiling.** Non-half-hourly customers are allocated to the half-hours by profile class, which is a published shape, not their real behaviour. Their real behaviour is recovered later, in aggregate, through reconciliation.

**Reconciliation runs.** Settlement is performed at intervals after the fact, each one replacing more estimated data with metered data, out beyond a year. A supplier receives charges and credits at each run.

**Why the clock matters commercially.** A margin computed on billed volume, on settled volume, and on cash actually banked are three different numbers for the same period. Reporting one without saying which is not a rounding difference — the gap can be large.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
**Imbalance prices should be extremely fat-tailed** — mostly unremarkable, occasionally orders of magnitude away. An imbalance series that looks like a tidy distribution is not an imbalance series.

**A supplier's settled volume for a past period should change between runs,** and the changes should shrink as the runs progress. If they do not shrink, the meter data is not improving.

**Estimated-read periods should reconcile with a visible correction** when a real read lands, and the size of that correction should grow with how long the estimate ran.

live_evidence.heading: What this simulation actually does
live_evidence.body:
The simulation settles half-hourly against the real published system prices and carries imbalance as a real cost line. Every published financial figure is labelled with its clock — settled, billed, or banked — because the three genuinely differ and a figure without its clock is treated here as a defect rather than a simplification.

Estimated versus actual meter reads are modelled per bill: Explore's fourth stage shows a household's actual bill with the read type on it, and the correction when a real read lands.

residuals.heading: What this page does not settle
residuals.body:
The full BSC reconciliation timetable is more elaborate than described here, and the simulation implements its economic consequence — that the number moves and the clocks differ — rather than every run and every deadline.

How much a domestic supplier's realised cost is driven by imbalance rather than by contracted cost depends heavily on how well it hedges volume, and this page does not put a number on it.

scope_delta.heading: Where the simulation stops
scope_delta.body: No Supplier Volume Allocation in its full detail. No modelling of the supplier's relationship with its own data collectors and aggregators. Reconciliation is modelled in its effect on the figures, not as the industry's full run calendar.
